claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant modified nucleotide in eukaryotic mRNA bodies.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant modified nucleotide in eukaryotic mRNA bodies.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: m6A is required for embryonic development and stem cell differentiation in several animals and plants.
source: It is required for embryonic development and stem cell differentiation in several animals and plants (Zhong et al., 2008; Batista et al., 2014; Ping et al., 2014; Geula et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017)
evidence: Multiple citations support this claim about the biological importance of m6A.

claim: m6A is required for control of the meiotic program in yeast.
source: and for the control of the meiotic program in yeast (Shah and Clancy, 1992; Clancy et al., 2002; Agarwala et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations support the role of m6A in yeast meiosis.

claim: Most N6-adenosine methylation of mRNA is catalyzed in the nucleus.
source: Most N6-adenosine methylation of mRNA is catalyzed in the nucleus (Salditt-Georgieff et al., 1976; Ke et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019)
evidence: Citations provide evidence for nuclear localization of m6A methylation.

claim: The catalytic core of the m6A writer consists of the heterodimer METTL3/METTL14 (MTA/MTB in plants).
source: by a highly conserved, multimeric methylase (the m6A 'writer'; Balacco and Soller, 2019) whose catalytic core consists of the heterodimer METTL3/METTL14 (MTA/MTB in plants; Bokar et al., 1997; Zhong et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations support the identity of the catalytic core of the m6A methyltransferase.

claim: m6A occurs in the consensus site RR(m6A)CH (R = G/A, H = A/C/U), primarily in 3′-UTRs in vertebrates, plants, and fungi that possess the canonical METTL3/METTL14 methyltransferase.
source: m6A occurs in the consensus site RR(m6A)CH (R = G/A, H = A/C/U), primarily in 3′-UTRs in vertebrates, plants, and fungi that possess the canonical METTL3/METTL14 methyltransferase (Bodi et al., 2012; Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Schwartz et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014a; Zhao et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2020; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: Multiple citations support the consensus sequence and location of m6A.

claim: The characteristic m6A motif and gene body location is not detected in organisms that lack METTL3/METTL14 homologs, such as C. elegans and bacteria.
source: Conversely, the characteristic motif and gene body location is not detected in organisms that lack METTL3/METTL14 homologs, such as the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (Sendinc et al., 2020) and bacteria (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations support the absence of the canonical m6A pattern in organisms lacking METTL3/METTL14.

claim: The YTH domain harbors a hydrophobic methyl-binding pocket that increases the affinity of m6A-containing RNA by more than 10-fold compared to unmethylated RNA.
source: The YTH domain harbors a hydrophobic methyl-binding pocket that increases the affinity of m6A-containing RNA by more than 10-fold compared to unmethylated RNA (Li et al., 2014b; Luo and Tong, 2014b; Theler et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations support the structural and functional properties of the YTH domain.

claim: YTH domain-RNA interactions mostly involve the sugar-phosphate backbone of the RNA.
source: Apart from interactions with the methylated adenosine and the purine at the –1 position, YTH domain-RNA interactions mostly involve the sugar-phosphate backbone of the RNA (Luo and Tong, 2014b; Theler et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: Citations support the mode of YTH domain-RNA interaction.

claim: The affinity of isolated YTH domains for m6A-containing RNA is modest, typically with dissociation constants on the order of 0.1–1 μM.
source: Because the affinity of isolated YTH domains for m6A-containing RNA is modest, typically with dissociation constants on the order of 0.1–1 μM (Li et al., 2014b; Luo and Tong, 2014b; Theler et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2014)
evidence: Citations provide quantitative data on YTH domain binding affinity.

claim: The YTHDF family comprises 11 proteins in Arabidopsis referred to as ECT1-11.
source: The YTHDF family comprises 11 proteins in Arabidopsis that are referred to as EVOLUTIONARILY CONSERVED C-TERMINAL REGION1-11 (ECT1-11) (Li et al., 2014c; Scutenaire et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations support the nomenclature and number of YTHDF proteins in Arabidopsis.

claim: ECT2, ECT3, and ECT4 are expressed in rapidly dividing cells of root, leaf, and flower primordia.
source: ECT2, ECT3, and ECT4 are expressed in rapidly dividing cells of root, leaf, and flower primordia, and genetic analyses have revealed their general importance in organogenesis (Arribas-Hernández et al., 2018; Arribas-Hernández et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations support the expression pattern and biological function of ECT2/3/4.

claim: The biological functions of ECT2/ECT3/ECT4 depend on intact m6A-binding pockets.
source: Importantly, the biological functions of ECT2/ECT3/ECT4 described thus far are shared with those of m6A writer components and, where tested, have been shown to depend on intact m6A-binding pockets, strongly suggesting that the basis for the observed phenotypes in ect2/ect3/ect4 mutants is defective regulation of m6A-modified mRNA targets (Bodi et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2016; Ružička et al., 2017; Arribas-Hernández et al., 2018; Scutenaire et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2018; Arribas-Hernández et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations support the m6A-dependence of ECT2/3/4 function.

claim: Wei et al., 2018 concluded that ECT2 binds to the 'plant-specific consensus motif' URU(m6A)Y.
source: In particular, this problem concerns the unexpected conclusion that ECT2 binds to the 'plant-specific consensus motif' URU(m6A)Y (Y = U/C), not RR(m6A)CH (Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation indicates a previous claim about ECT2 binding specificity.

claim: Several motifs including URUAY, UGUAMM, UGWAMH, UGUAWA, and GGAU have been reported to be enriched around m6A sites in Arabidopsis and other plant species.
source: To complicate matters further, a number of motifs including not only URUAY, but also UGUAMM (M = A/C), UGWAMH (W = A/U), UGUAWA, and GGAU have been reported to be enriched around m6A sites in Arabidopsis and other plant species (Li et al., 2014a; Anderson et al., 2018; Miao et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019)
evidence: Citations support the reported enrichment of various motifs around m6A sites.

claim: ADARcd fusions to ECT2 are functional in vivo as demonstrated by rescue of te234 mutant seedling phenotypes.
source: We identified lines exhibiting nearly complete rescue of te234 mutant seedling phenotypes, indicating that the fusion protein was functional (Figure 1A).
evidence: Phenotypic rescue demonstrates functionality of the fusion protein.

claim: The ECT2-FLAG-ADAR fusion imparts adenosine-to-inosine editing of target mRNAs in planta.
source: This revealed that the amount of editing was clearly higher in the lines expressing the ECT2-FLAG-ADAR fusion protein than in the negative control lines (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Data shows differential editing between fusion and control lines.

claim: HyperTRIBE identified 16,176 edited sites in aerial tissues and 19,242 in roots, corresponding to 4864 and 5052 genes (ECT2 HT-targets), respectively.
source: Application of subsequent filtering steps, including removal of non-(A-to-G) mismatches and of potential line-specific single-nucleotide variants (see Materials and methods), resulted in a final list of 16,176 edited sites for aerial tissues and 19,242 for roots, corresponding to 4864 and 5052 genes (ECT2 HT-targets), respectively (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Data analysis pipeline yielded specific numbers of edited sites and target genes.

claim: More than 76% of ECT2 HT-targets had m6A support by either Shen et al., 2016 or Parker et al., 2020 studies.
source: Of most importance, we observed a large overlap between the ECT2 HT-targets and m6A-containing transcripts mapped by different methods in seedlings (Shen et al., 2016; Parker et al., 2020) as more than 76% of ECT2 HT-targets had m6A support by either study (Figure 2D).
evidence: Overlap analysis with independent m6A datasets validates HyperTRIBE results.

claim: ECT2-mCherry can be specifically UV-crosslinked to target RNA in vivo.
source: These tests showed that substantially more RNA co-purifies with wild-type ECT2 than with ECT2W464A upon UV-crosslinking, and that no RNA is detected without UV irradiation or from irradiated plants of non-transgenic backgrounds (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data demonstrates specific UV-crosslinking of ECT2 to RNA.

claim: A total of 15,960 iCLIP peaks or crosslink sites in 2281 genes were identified from the 110-kDa band of wild-type ECT2-mCherry.
source: We identified a total of 15,960 iCLIP 'peaks' or crosslink sites (i.e., single-nucleotide positions called by PureCLIP from mapped iCLIP reads [Krakau et al., 2017]) in 2281 genes from the 110-kDa band of wild-type ECT2-mCherry (henceforth referred to as ECT2 iCLIP peaks and targets, respectively).
evidence: Data analysis of iCLIP sequencing yielded specific numbers of peaks and target genes.

claim: The majority of ECT2 iCLIP crosslink sites mapped to the 3′-UTRs of mRNAs.
source: Importantly, for both libraries, the majority of crosslink sites mapped to the 3′-UTRs of mRNAs (Figure 3H, see Figure 4A, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for more examples), coincident with the main location of m6A (Figure 4B; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: Data shows enrichment of crosslink sites in 3'-UTRs, consistent with m6A location.

claim: ECT2 iCLIP targets and HyperTRIBE targets showed clear overlaps with each other and with m6A-containing transcripts.
source: ECT2 targets identified by iCLIP and HyperTRIBE showed clear overlaps, both with each other and with m6A-containing transcripts, further supporting the robustness of ECT2 target identification via combined iCLIP and HyperTRIBE approaches (Figure 4D, upper panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Overlap analysis demonstrates consistency between orthogonal methods.

claim: HyperTRIBE identifies approximately three times more ECT2 targets than iCLIP.
source: We also observed that HyperTRIBE identifies approximately three times more ECT2 targets than iCLIP, possibly because of the bias towards high abundance inherent to purification-based methods like iCLIP (Wheeler et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison of target numbers between methods reveals differential sensitivity.

claim: ECT2 crosslinks in the immediate vicinity, but preferentially upstream (~11 nt) of Nanopore-determined m6A sites.
source: This analysis showed that ECT2 crosslinks in the immediate vicinity, but preferentially upstream (~11 nt) of Nanopore-determined m6A sites, with a mild depletion at the exact m6A site (Figure 5A, upper panel).
evidence: Positional analysis of iCLIP data relative to m6A sites reveals spatial relationship.

claim: UV illumination used in both iCLIP and miCLIP preferentially generates RNA-protein crosslinks involving uridine.
source: This pattern is probably explained by the fact that the UV illumination used in both iCLIP and miCLIP preferentially generates RNA-protein crosslinks involving uridine (Hafner et al., 2021), also detectable in the datasets analyzed here (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Citation and data analysis support UV crosslinking bias towards uridine.

claim: RRACH-like motifs and GGAU were the most highly enriched at m6A sites.
source: Not surprisingly, RRACH-like motifs were the most highly enriched at m6A sites and showed a clear enrichment immediately downstream of ECT2 crosslink sites in our analyses, with the degenerate variant DRACH being the most frequently observed (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3). Motifs containing GGAU behaved similarly to DRACH, with a sharp enrichment exactly at m6A sites and mild enrichment downstream of ECT2 peaks (Figure 5D)
evidence: Motif enrichment analysis identifies RRACH/DRACH and GGAU as most enriched at m6A sites.

claim: U/Y-rich motifs showed a characteristic enrichment around, but depletion at, m6A sites.
source: U/R-rich motifs without traces of adjacent DRACH (e.g., YUGUM, URUAY, URURU) showed a characteristic enrichment around, but depletion at, m6A sites.
evidence: Motif distribution analysis reveals distinct pattern for U/Y-rich motifs.

claim: DRACH/GGAU motifs at the site and flanking U/Y-rich sequences are the main determinants for distinguishing m6A sites from background.
source: The top 16 features ordered by importance from the full model confirmed that RRAC/DRACH or GGAU at the site was indicative of the presence of m6A (Figure 6B). Interestingly, U/Y-rich sequences (UNUNU and YYYYY in particular) flanking the site were also strongly indicative (Figure 6B).
evidence: Machine learning analysis identifies key sequence features distinguishing m6A sites.

claim: Flanking U/Y-rich sequences are the main determinants for ECT2 crosslinking at m6A sites.
source: In agreement with previous observations, this model showed flanking U/Y-rich sequences as the main determinants for ECT2 crosslinking (Figure 6D).
evidence: Machine learning analysis identifies U/Y-rich sequences as key for ECT2 binding.

claim: If a transcript has m6A and ECT2 sites in close proximity, it is more likely to have UNUNU/UUUUU/YYYYY sequences upstream of the m6A site.
source: If a transcript has m6A and ECT2 sites in close proximity, it is (1) more likely to have UNUNU/UUUUU/YYYYY sequences upstream of the m6A site than targets with distantly located ECT2-binding sites or than non-ECT2 targets
evidence: Comparative analysis of motif distributions reveals association between specific U-rich motifs and ECT2 binding proximity.

claim: Transcripts with m6A and ECT2 sites in close proximity are less likely to have URURU/URUAY-like motifs upstream of the m6A site.
source: (3) less likely to have URURU/URUAY-like motifs upstream of the m6A site.
evidence: Comparative analysis reveals negative association between URURU/URUAY motifs and ECT2 binding.

claim: The 5′–3′ asymmetry of ECT2 peaks relative to m6A sites observed with full-length ECT2 was largely reduced with the truncated protein lacking the IDR.
source: Initial inspection of the distribution of ECT2 peaks relative to Nanopore-m6A sites showed that the 5′–3′ asymmetry observed with full-length ECT2 was largely reduced with the truncated protein (Figure 7C), as was the bias towards uridines (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Comparison of full-length and truncated ECT2 iCLIP data reveals role of IDR in binding pattern.

claim: UUUUUU/UNUNU-like motifs were more enriched at and immediately upstream of IDR-dependent crosslink sites relative to IDR-independent ones.
source: UUUUUU/UNUNU-like motifs were more enriched at and immediately upstream of IDR-dependent crosslink sites relative to the IDR-independent ones, supporting preferential crosslinking of the IDR to Us in this region.
evidence: Analysis of IDR-dependent vs. IDR-independent crosslink sites reveals IDR binding preferences.

claim: URURU/URUAY motifs showed modest depletion 5′ to IDR-dependent crosslink sites relative to their IDR-independent counterparts.
source: Remarkably, the exact opposite was true for URURU/URUAY motifs that showed modest depletion 5′ to IDR-dependent crosslink sites relative to their IDR-independent counterparts (Figure 7D).
evidence: Analysis reveals distinct behavior of URURU/URUAY motifs relative to IDR-dependent binding.

claim: ECT2 binds to m6A predominantly in the DR(m6A)CH sequence context in vivo.
source: It is a major conclusion of the present work that ECT2 binds to m6A predominantly in the DR(m6A)CH sequence context in vivo, consistent with reading of m6A written by the conserved nuclear MTA/MTB methyltransferase.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence from iCLIP and motif analysis support this conclusion.

claim: The IDR of ECT2 participates in RNA binding by association with U-rich elements.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the IDR of ECT2 participates in locating ECT2 to 3′-UTRs by association with U-rich elements.
evidence: Multiple observations from iCLIP experiments with full-length and truncated ECT2 support IDR involvement in RNA binding.

claim: URUAY may be a site of competition between the IDR of ECT2 and another, as yet unknown, RNA-binding protein.
source: Although these observations may be explained by multiple scenarios, we find a simple, yet at present speculative, model attractive: URUAY may be a site of competition between the IDR of ECT2 and another, as yet unknown, RNA-binding protein.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observed data patterns.

claim: FA-CLIP is not a recommendable technique for identification of RNAs associating with RNA-binding proteins.
source: Finally, our work also clearly indicates that FA-CLIP, now used in at least two studies involving YTH domain proteins (Wei et al., 2018; Song et al., 2021), is not a recommendable technique as it recovers many false positives and fails to include many genuine targets.
evidence: Comparison of FA-CLIP results with iCLIP and HyperTRIBE data reveals limitations of FA-CLIP.

claim: DRACH is the major N6-adenosine methylation site.
source: First, the major N6-adenosine methylation site is DRACH, consistent with conclusions from multiple other studies.
evidence: Motif enrichment analysis and consistency with literature support this conclusion.

claim: GGAU is a minor N6-adenosine methylation site.
source: Second, GGAU is a minor N6-adenosine methylation site, as seen by its enrichment directly at m6A sites.
evidence: Motif enrichment analysis at m6A sites supports this conclusion.

claim: m6A occurs in DRACH/GGAU islands embedded in U-rich regions.
source: Third, m6A occurs in DRACH/GGAU islands embedded in U-rich regions.
evidence: Motif distribution analysis reveals this pattern.

claim: U-rich regions around m6A sites are of similar importance for recognition of m6A-containing transcripts as DRACH and GGAU at m6A sites.
source: Such U-rich regions around m6A sites emerged from sorting of methylated from non-methylated transcripts by machine learning as being of similar importance for recognition of m6A-containing transcripts from sequence features as DRACH and GGAU at m6A sites, suggesting their implication in MTA/MTB-catalyzed adenosine methylation (Figure 6C).
evidence: Machine learning analysis reveals importance of U-rich regions for m6A site identification.

claim: The pronounced 3′-UTR bias of m6A occurrence may be explained by the rarity of extensive poly-U and poly-pyrimidine tracts in coding regions.
source: This, in turn, may also explain the pronounced 3′-UTR bias of m6A occurrence as extensive poly-U and poly-pyrimidine tracts are rare in coding regions (Figure 5D, second row on the right-most column; Supplementary file 3, page 1).
evidence: Analysis of motif distribution across gene regions supports this inference.

claim: The tendency of m6A to occur at stop codons can be explained by UAA and UGA stop codons corresponding to DRA, increasing the frequency of DRACH directly at stop codons.
source: As a special case in this context, our analyses suggest a simple explanation for the tendency of m6A to occur at stop codons. UAA and UGA correspond to DRA, increasing the frequency of occurrence of DRACH directly at stop codons (Figure 5D, second row on the left-most column), many of which have adjacent U-rich elements in the 3′-UTRs.
evidence: Sequence analysis and motif enrichment at stop codons support this explanation.

claim: This work refutes the claim by Wei et al., 2018 that ECT2 binds to the supposedly plant-specific m6A-containing sequence motif URU(m6A)Y.
source: This key conclusion refutes the claim by Wei et al., 2018 that ECT2 binds to the supposedly plant-specific m6A-containing sequence motif URU(m6A)Y, and it thereby reconciles knowledge on m6A-YTHDF axes in plants specifically and in eukaryotes more broadly.
evidence: The comprehensive data from iCLIP and HyperTRIBE contradicts the previous FA-CLIP-based conclusion.

claim: The IDR of ECT2 limits accessibility of 5′ ends of bound mRNAs to polynucleotide kinase.
source: First, RNA complexes with YTH-mCherry were 5′-labeled by polynucleotide kinase much more efficiently than RNA complexes with full-length ECT2-mCherry, indicating that the IDR limits accessibility to the 5′ of bound mRNAs.
evidence: Differential labeling efficiency between full-length and truncated ECT2 supports this conclusion.

claim: The full-length ECT2W464A-mCherry mutant retained an enrichment of crosslink sites in 3′-UTRs, in contrast to the m6A-binding-deficient YTHW464A-mCherry truncation.
source: Second, in contrast to the m6A-binding-deficient YTHW464A-mCherry truncation, the full-length ECT2W464A-mCherry mutant retained an enrichment of crosslink sites in 3′-UTRs.
evidence: Comparison of crosslink site distributions between different ECT2 variants supports IDR-mediated 3'-UTR binding.

claim: Crosslinks specific to the IDR are mainly 5′ to m6A sites and cause an asymmetric distribution of ECT2 crosslink sites around m6A sites.
source: Third, crosslinks specific to the IDR (i.e., observed only with full-length ECT2-mCherry-RNA complexes, but not with YTH-Cherry-RNA complexes), could be assigned and have two notable properties. They are mainly 5′ to m6A sites, and thereby cause a conspicuously asymmetric distribution of ECT2 crosslink sites around m6A sites, not seen with crosslinks to the YTH-mCherry fragment.
evidence: Comparison of crosslink distributions between full-length and truncated ECT2 reveals IDR-specific binding pattern.

claim: IDR-specific crosslinks are specifically enriched in U-rich elements of the type UUUUUU and UNUNU immediately upstream of m6A sites.
source: In addition, the IDR-specific crosslinks are specifically enriched in U-rich elements of the type UUUUUU and UNUNU immediately upstream.
evidence: Motif enrichment analysis of IDR-specific crosslink sites reveals this pattern.

claim: Diverging IDRs among YTHDF paralogs could confer target specificity via binding to distinct motifs in the vicinity of m6A sites.
source: Similarly, it is possible that diverging IDRs among YTHDF paralogs could confer target specificity via binding to distinct motifs in the vicinity of m6A sites, such that specific YTHDF-target mRNA repertoires could exist even for YTHDF proteins coexpressed in the same cells.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings about ECT2 IDR function.

claim: URUAY has three properties suggesting ties to ECT2 binding: it crosslinks to ECT2 when present 5′ to m6A sites, it is more enriched close to m6A sites without ECT2 binding, and its enrichment 5′ to ECT2 crosslink sites is observed only for IDR-independent crosslinks.
source: In contrast to other m6A-proximal, pyrimidine-rich sequences (e.g., UNUNU, YYYYY) that may be of importance for both m6A writing and ECT2 binding, URUAY appears to have ties more specifically to ECT2 binding thanks to three properties. (1) When present 5′ to m6A sites, it crosslinks to ECT2, suggesting that some part of the protein can be in contact with URUAY. (2) URUAY is more enriched close to m6A sites for which there is no evidence of ECT2 binding, suggesting that it weakens ECT2 binding. This latter point is also consistent with the distinction of ECT2-bound from non-ECT2-bound m6A sites by machine learning that did not find URUAY to be of importance for ECT2-bound sites. (3) The URUAY enrichment 5′ to ECT2 crosslink sites is observed only when crosslinks to both full-length protein and the YTH-mCherry fragment are considered (IDR-independent), but disappears when crosslinks specific to the full-length protein (IDR-dependent) are analyzed.
evidence: Multiple analyses of URUAY motif distribution and association with ECT2 binding support these properties.

claim: The functional dissection of the URUAY element in m6A reading constitutes a subject of major importance, emphasized by the broad conservation of its enrichment around m6A sites across multiple plant species.
source: In any event, the functional dissection of the URUAY element in m6A reading now constitutes a subject of major importance, emphasized by the broad conservation of its enrichment around m6A sites across multiple plant species, including rice (Li et al., 2014a; Zhang et al., 2019), maize (Luo et al., 2020; Miao et al., 2020), tomato (Zhou et al., 2019), and Arabidopsis (Miao et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations support the conservation of URUAY enrichment across plant species.
